description: Some species seem to defy death. Jellyfish that rejuvenate, hydras without aging: the secret is in cellular repair.

hero.hook: Aging is not an absolute law of life. Some species have found the fault.

blocks.text: We grow old, then we die. However, the  jellyfish can return to a juvenile stage and start again. The clam **Ming** lived **507 years**. Aging is therefore not a universal rule: it is a process that certain species circumvent. [[Turritopsis dohrnii]]
By studying these exceptions, researchers are looking less for science fiction immortality than for tricks of life to better repair cells.
Aging is not just about “wearing out” like a machine. It's an imbalance: damage accumulates faster than repairs.

blocks.caption: Telomeres, at the ends of chromosomes, shorten with each cell division.

blocks.text: At the ends of our chromosomes,  act like shoelace tips. With each cell division, they shorten. Too short, the cell stops dividing. At the same time, metabolism produces aggressive molecules which damage proteins and DNA. “Zombie” cells then accumulate and inflame the tissues around them. [[Telomeres]]
The tardigrade, a tiny “water bear”, can almost stop living by drying out. His metabolism drops to **99.99%**, and he survives the vacuum of space or extreme radiation without truly aging.

The injured or starved  transforms its adult cells into “blank” cells, then becomes a polyp again, the starting stage. This step back, called transdifferentiation, gives it a form of **biological immortality**. [[Turritopsis dohrnii]]

The **hydra**, a small freshwater polyp, renews its entire body thanks to an almost unlimited supply of . She shows no measurable signs of aging. The bowhead whale can exceed **200 years** thanks to ultra-efficient DNA repair and strong resistance to cancer. [[stem cells]]
Lobsters make telomerase everywhere in their bodies: their telomeres do not shorten. They grow throughout their lives and die especially when molting becomes too costly.

The idea is no longer just to treat Alzheimer's or osteoarthritis one by one, but to attack aging itself. **senolytics** aim to eliminate zombie cells. In animals, this has already rejuvenated certain functions.

Limiting calories without malnutrition also activates repair pathways, notably by slowing down , a protein that accelerates growth… and sometimes decline. Other labs are trying to “wind the clock” of cells, like jellyfish, without transforming them into tumors. [[mTOR]]
Even a biologically immortal species dies from predators, disease, or disaster. Death remains a driving force of evolution: it gives way to new, better adapted generations.
For humans, the realistic challenge is not to live forever, but to extend the years **in good health**. Longevity turned technology would also raise huge questions of equity and resources.
Biological immortality relies on repairing or resetting cells. The Turritopsis dohrnii jellyfish is getting younger; the hydra is constantly renewing itself. Aging is not a universal fatality.
